title: The Return of Ulysses
paragraphs: As darkness fell, the Rat, looking excited and mysterious, called them back into the parlor, lined each of them up next to his own little pile, and began to outfit them for the coming expedition. He took it all very seriously and thoroughly, and the business ate up a good deal of time. First came a belt for each animal, then a sword to stick into each belt, then a cutlass on the other side to balance it. After that came a pair of pistols, a policeman’s truncheon, several pairs of handcuffs, some bandages and sticking plaster, and a flask and a sandwich case. The Badger laughed good-naturedly and said, “All right, Ratty! It keeps you happy and it doesn’t hurt me. I’m going to do everything I have to do with this stick right here.” But the Rat only said, “_Please_, Badger. I wouldn’t want you to blame me afterward and say I’d forgotten _something!_”

When everything was finally ready, the Badger picked up a dark lantern in one paw, gripped his big stick in the other, and said, “Right, follow me! Mole goes first, “cos I’m very pleased with him; Rat next; Toad last. And listen here, Toady! Don’t chatter the way you usually do, or you’ll be sent back, as sure as anything!”

Toad was so afraid of being left out that he accepted his lowly place without a murmur, and the animals set off. The Badger led them a short way along the river, then suddenly swung himself over the edge and into a hole in the riverbank, a little above the water. The Mole and the Rat followed in silence, swinging into the hole successfully, just as they had watched the Badger do. But when Toad’s turn came, of course he slipped and fell into the water with a loud splash and a squeal of alarm. His friends hauled him out, rubbed him down, wrung him out in a hurry, comforted him, and stood him back on his feet. But the Badger was truly angry, and told him that the very next time he made a fool of himself he would certainly be left behind.
And so at last they were inside the secret passage, and the expedition to take back the house had truly begun!

The tunnel was cold, dark, damp, low and narrow, and poor Toad started to shiver—partly out of dread at what might be waiting ahead, and partly because he was soaked to the skin. The lantern was a long way in front, and in the blackness he kept slipping a little behind. Then he heard Rat call back in warning, “_Come_ on, Toad!” and such terror seized him at the thought of being abandoned alone in the dark that he “came on” at a headlong rush, and crashed the Rat into the Mole and the Mole into the Badger, and for a moment nobody knew which way was up. The Badger took it for an attack from the rear, and since there was no space to swing a stick or a cutlass, he whipped out a pistol and was about to put a bullet in Toad. When he learned what had truly happened, he was furious, and said, “Well, this time that wretched Toad _shall_ be left behind!”

But Toad whimpered, and the other two promised to answer for his good behavior, and at last the Badger calmed down and the procession moved on. Only this time the Rat marched at the back, keeping a firm grip on Toad’s shoulder.
So they felt their way and shuffled along, ears pricked up and paws resting on their pistols, until at last the Badger said, “We should be just about underneath the Hall by now.”

Then suddenly they heard a confused rumble of sound, which seemed far away and yet also almost directly over their heads, as if people were shouting and cheering and stamping on the floor and banging on tables. Toad’s nervous terrors all came back, but the Badger just remarked calmly, “They _are_ carrying on, those Weasels!”

The tunnel started to climb. They groped forward a bit farther, and the racket broke out once more, plainly this time and right overhead. “Hoo-ray-hooray-hoo-ray-hooray!” they heard, with the drumming of little feet on the floor and the clink of glasses as small fists banged on a table. “_What_ a time they’re having!” said the Badger. “Come on!” They hurried until the passage ended abruptly, and they found themselves under the trapdoor leading up into the butler’s pantry.

Such a tremendous racket was going on in the banqueting hall that there was little risk of anyone overhearing them. The Badger said, “Now, boys, all together!” and the four of them set their shoulders against the trap door and heaved it back. Boosting one another up, they found themselves standing in the pantry, with only a door between them and the banqueting hall, where their unsuspecting enemies were carousing.

Coming out of the passage, they were met by a din that was positively deafening. At last, as the cheers and hammering gradually faded, one voice rose out of it: “Well, I don’t mean to keep you much longer”—(great applause)—“but before I take my seat”—(renewed cheering)—“I’d like to say a word about our generous host, Mr. Toad. We all know Toad!”—(great laughter)—“_Good_ Toad, _modest_ Toad, _honest_ Toad!” (shrieks of merriment).
“Just let me get my hands on him!” muttered Toad, grinding his teeth.
“Hold on a minute!” said the Badger, barely managing to hold him back. “Get ready, all of you!”
“—Let me sing you a little song,” the voice went on, “which I have composed about Toad”—(prolonged applause).
Then the Chief Weasel—for it was he—began in a high, squeaky voice—

“Toad he went out on a spree
Happily down the street—”
The Badger drew himself up, gripped his stick firmly in both paws, glanced around at his comrades, and cried—
“The hour has come! Follow me!”
And he threw the door wide open.
Goodness!
What a squealing and squeaking and screeching filled the air!

No wonder the terrified weasels dove under the tables and leaped wildly at the windows! No wonder the ferrets dashed madly for the fireplace and got hopelessly stuck in the chimney! No wonder tables and chairs were overturned, and glass and china went crashing to the floor, in the panic of that dreadful moment when the four Heroes strode angrily into the room! There was the mighty Badger, whiskers bristling, his great club whistling through the air; Mole, black and grim, waving his stick and shouting his awful war cry, “A Mole! A Mole!” Rat, desperate and determined, his belt bulging with weapons of every age and every kind; Toad, frantic with excitement and wounded pride, swollen to twice his usual size, leaping into the air and letting out Toad-whoops that chilled them to the bone! “Toad he went out on a spree!” he yelled. “_I’ll_ give them a spree!” and he went straight for the Chief Weasel. There were only four of them in all, but to the panic-stricken weasels the hall seemed full of monstrous animals, gray, black, brown and yellow, whooping and swinging enormous clubs. They broke and fled with squeals of terror and dismay, this way and that, out the windows, up the chimney, anywhere to get out of reach of those terrible sticks.

It was over quickly. The four Friends strode up and down the whole length of the hall, cracking their sticks down on every head that popped up, and within five minutes the room was empty of foes. From beyond the smashed windows came the faint shrieks of terrified weasels scurrying off across the lawn. Some dozen of the enemy lay sprawled on the floor, and the Mole was busy snapping handcuffs onto them. The Badger paused from his labors, leaned on his stick, and mopped his honest brow.

“Mole,” he said,” “you’re the best of fellows! Just slip outside and keep an eye on those stoat sentries of yours, and see what they’re up to. I have an idea that, thanks to you, we won’t have much trouble from _them_ tonight!”

The Mole promptly vanished through a window. The Badger ordered the other two to stand a table back on its legs, gather up the knives, forks, plates and glasses from the _wreckage_ on the floor, and hunt around for the makings of a supper. “I want some grub, I do,” he said, in the rather common way he had of speaking. “Get a move on, Toad, look lively! We’ve won your house back for you, and you haven’t offered us so much as a sandwich.” Toad was a bit hurt that the Badger had no kind words for him, the way he had for the Mole—no telling him what a fine fellow he was or how magnificently he’d fought. After all, he was especially pleased with himself, and with how he had charged the Chief Weasel and sent him flying over the table with a single blow of his stick. Still, he bustled about, and so did the Rat, and before long they turned up some guava jelly in a glass dish, a cold chicken, a hardly touched tongue, some trifle, and a good deal of lobster salad. In the pantry they also found a basket of French rolls and plenty of cheese, butter and celery. They were just about to sit down when the Mole came scrambling in through the window, chuckling, with an armful of rifles.

“It’s all over,” he reported. “As far as I can make out, the stoats were already very nervous and jumpy, and as soon as they heard the shrieks and yells and uproar inside the hall, some of them threw down their rifles and ran. The others stood their ground for a bit, but when the weasels came rushing out at them they thought they’d been betrayed. So the stoats grabbed the weasels, and the weasels struggled to get away, and they wrestled and wriggled and punched each other and rolled over and over, until most of ’em rolled into the river! They’ve all disappeared by now, one way or another, and I’ve got their rifles. So _that’s_ all taken care of!”

“Excellent, deserving animal!” said the Badger, his mouth stuffed with chicken and trifle. “Now, there’s one last thing I need from you, Mole, before you sit down to supper with the rest of us. I wouldn’t bother you with it, but I know you’re the one to trust to get a thing done, and I wish I could say that of everybody I know. I’d send Rat, if he weren’t a poet. Take those fellows lying on the floor up the stairs with you, and have some bedrooms swept out, tidied and made properly comfortable. Be sure they sweep _under_ the beds, put on fresh sheets and pillowcases, and fold one corner of the bedclothes back, just the way you know it should be done. Put a can of hot water, clean towels and new cakes of soap in every room. After that you may give each of them a good licking, if it would satisfy you, and send them off through the back door—we shan’t be seeing any more of _them_, I fancy. Then come back and have some of this cold tongue. It’s first-rate. I’m very pleased with you, Mole!”

The good-natured Mole took up a stick, lined his prisoners up in a row on the floor, barked “Quick march!” and marched his squad off upstairs. Some time later he came back, smiling, to report that every room was ready and as neat as a new pin. “And I didn’t have to lick them, either,” he added. “I figured they’d been licked enough for one night, on the whole, and when I put the point to the weasels they quite agreed, and said they wouldn’t dream of putting me to the trouble. They were very contrite and said they were terribly sorry for what they’d done, but it was all the fault of the Chief Weasel and the stoats, and if there was ever anything they could do for us to make amends, we had only to say so. So I handed each of them a roll and let them out the back, and off they bolted as fast as their legs would carry them!”

Then the Mole drew his chair up to the table and dug into the cold tongue, and Toad, gentleman that he was, set aside all his jealousy and said warmly, “Thank you kindly, dear Mole, for all your pains and trouble tonight, and above all for your cleverness this morning!” This pleased the Badger, who answered, “There spoke my brave Toad!” And so, in great joy and contentment, they finished supper and soon retired to bed between clean sheets, safe in Toad’s ancestral home, which they had won back by peerless valor, consummate strategy, and a proper way with sticks.

Toad, who as usual had slept far too long, came down to breakfast the next morning shamefully late. What he found on the table was a quantity of eggshells, a few crusts of cold, rubbery toast, a coffeepot three-quarters empty, and really not much else—which did little for his temper, since it was, after all, his own house. Out through the French windows of the breakfast room he could see the Mole and the Water Rat in wicker chairs on the lawn, evidently trading stories, roaring with laughter and kicking their short legs in the air. The Badger sat in an armchair, deep in the morning paper, and only glanced up and nodded as Toad came in. But Toad knew his man; he sat down, made the best breakfast he could, and merely told himself that he would get even with the others sooner or later. When he was nearly done, the Badger looked up and said rather shortly, “I’m sorry, Toad, but I’m afraid you’ve got a heavy morning’s work ahead. We really ought to hold a Banquet right away, you see, to celebrate this affair. It’s expected of you—in fact, it’s the rule.”

“Oh, very well!” Toad said at once. “Anything to oblige. Mind you, I can’t imagine why anybody would hold a Banquet in the morning. But you know I live for no one’s pleasure but my friends’—I simply find out what they want and then arrange it for ’em, you dear old Badger!”

“Don’t play stupider than you are,” the Badger replied crossly, “and stop chuckling and spluttering into your coffee while you talk; it’s bad manners. What I mean is that the Banquet will be at night, naturally, but the invitations must be written and sent off right away, and you’re the one to write them. Now sit down at that table—you’ll find stacks of letter paper there, with ‘Toad Hall’ across the top in blue and gold—and write invitations to all our friends. If you stick to it, we’ll have them out before lunch. And _I’ll_ pitch in too, and take my share of the load. _I’ll_ order the Banquet.”

“What!” Toad cried, aghast. “Me, cooped up inside scratching out a pile of rotten letters on a glorious morning like this, when what I want is to tour my estate, put every creature and every corner right, and strut and enjoy myself! Certainly not! I’ll be—I’ll see you——Wait just a moment, though! Why, of course, dear Badger! What are my pleasure and comfort beside those of other people! You want it done, and done it shall be. Off you go, Badger, order the Banquet, order anything you please; then run along and join our young friends outdoors in their innocent fun, and never mind poor me with my cares and toils. I give up this lovely morning on the altar of duty and friendship!”

The Badger eyed him with deep suspicion, but Toad’s frank, open face made it hard to accuse him of any bad motive behind this change of heart. So he left the room and headed for the kitchen, and the moment the door shut behind him, Toad rushed to the writing desk. A wonderful idea had struck him while he was talking. He _would_ write the invitations! He would make sure to mention the leading part he had played in the fight, and how he had knocked the Chief Weasel flat. He would hint at his adventures and the whole triumphant career he had to tell about. And on the back he would set out a sort of program of entertainment for the evening—something like this, as he sketched it in his head:—
SPEECH. . . . BY TOAD. (TOAD will deliver further speeches in the course of the evening.)
ADDRESS. . . BY TOAD SYNOPSIS—Our Prison System—the Waterways of Old England—Horse-dealing, and How to Deal—Property, Its Rights and Its Duties—Back to the Land—A Typical English Squire.
SONG. . . . BY TOAD. (Written by himself.)
OTHER COMPOSITIONS. BY TOAD will be sung in the course of the evening by the. . . COMPOSER.

The idea delighted him enormously, and he worked so hard that all the letters were finished by noon. Just then he was told that a small, rather bedraggled weasel was at the door, timidly asking whether he could be of any help to the gentlemen. Toad strutted out and found one of the prisoners from the night before, very respectful and eager to please. He patted him on the head, pushed the bundle of invitations into his paw, and told him to run along quickly and deliver them as fast as he could; and if he cared to come back in the evening, there might be a shilling for him, or then again there might not. The poor weasel seemed truly grateful, and hurried off eagerly to do his errand.

When the other animals came back for lunch, noisy and windblown after a morning on the river, Mole, whose conscience had been nagging him, looked uneasily at Toad, expecting to find him sulking or low. Instead Toad was so cocky and puffed up that Mole began to suspect something, while Rat and Badger traded meaningful looks.

The moment the meal ended, Toad pushed his paws deep into his trouser pockets, tossed out a careless “Well, look after yourselves, you fellows! Ask for anything you want!” and began to swagger off toward the garden, meaning to think up an idea or two for his coming speeches, when the Rat grabbed him by the arm.

Toad had a fair idea what Rat was after and did his best to slip away, but when Badger firmly took his other arm, he saw that the game was up. The two of them marched him into the small smoking room off the entrance hall, shut the door, and sat him down in a chair. Then they both stood in front of him, while Toad sat silent, looking at them with great suspicion and bad temper.

“Now, look here, Toad,” said the Rat. “This is about the Banquet, and I’m very sorry to have to speak to you this way. But we need you to understand, plainly and once and for all, that there will be no speeches and no songs. Get it into your head that this time we aren’t arguing with you—we’re just telling you.”
Toad realized he was caught in a trap. The others knew him too well; they had seen through him and beaten him to it. All his lovely daydreams lay in ruins.
“Can’t I sing them just one _little_ song?” he begged pitifully.

“No, not _one_ little song,” the Rat answered firmly, though his heart ached at the sight of poor disappointed Toad’s trembling lip. “It’s no good, Toady. You know very well that your songs are nothing but conceit and boasting and vanity, and your speeches are nothing but self-praise and—and—well, shameless exaggeration and—and——”
“And hot air,” put in Badger, in his blunt way.

“It’s for your own good, Toady,” the Rat went on. “You know you _must_ turn over a new leaf sooner or later, and this looks like a splendid moment to start—a kind of turning point in your career. And please don’t think that saying all this doesn’t hurt me more than it hurts you.”

Toad sat sunk in thought for a long while. At last he raised his head, and strong emotion showed plainly on his face. “You have won, my friends,” he said in a broken voice. “It was only a small thing I asked—merely permission to blossom and expand for one more evening, to let myself go and hear the thunderous applause that always seems to me—somehow—to bring out my best qualities. But you are right, I know, and I am wrong. From now on I will be a very different Toad. My friends, you will never have cause to blush for me again. But oh dear, oh dear, this is a hard world!”
And pressing his handkerchief to his face, he left the room with faltering steps.
“Badger,” said the Rat, “_I_ feel like a brute. I wonder how _you_ feel?”

“Oh, I know, I know,” the Badger said gloomily. “But it had to be done. This good fellow has to live here, stand on his own feet, and command respect. Would you want him to be a common laughingstock, mocked and jeered at by stoats and weasels?”

“Of course not,” said the Rat. “And since we’re on the subject of weasels, it’s lucky we ran into that little fellow just as he set off with Toad’s invitations. Something you’d told me made me suspicious, so I peeked at a couple of them, and they were downright shameful. I confiscated the lot, and our good Mole is now installed in the blue boudoir, writing out plain, simple invitation cards instead.”

At last the hour of the banquet drew near, and Toad, who had gone up to his bedroom after leaving the others, was still sitting there, gloomy and thoughtful. With his brow resting on his paw, he pondered long and deeply. Gradually his face cleared, and he began to smile long, slow smiles. Then he started giggling in a shy, self-conscious way. At last he got up, locked the door, drew the curtains across the windows, gathered all the chairs in the room and set them in a semicircle, and took his place in front of them, visibly swelling. Then he bowed, coughed twice, and, letting himself go, sang at the top of his voice to the enraptured audience that his imagination saw so clearly.
TOAD’S LAST LITTLE SONG!

The Toad—came—home!
Panic ran through the parlors and howls rang through the halls,
There was weeping in the cowsheds and screaming in the stalls,
When the Toad—came—home!

When the Toad—came—home!
There was smashing of the windows and crashing of the doors,
There was chasing after weasels who fainted on the floors,
When the Toad—came—home!

Boom! go the drums!
The trumpeters are tooting, the soldiers are saluting,
The cannons are all shooting and the motorcars are hooting,
As the—Hero—comes!

Shout—Hooray!
And let everyone in the crowd try to shout it very loud,
In honor of an animal of whom you’re rightly proud,
For it’s Toad’s—great—day!
He sang it at the top of his voice, with tremendous feeling and flourish, and when he was finished he started right in and sang it all over again.
Then he heaved a deep sigh, a long, long, long sigh.

After that, he wet his hairbrush in the water jug, parted his hair down the middle, and slicked it flat and shiny on either side of his face. Then he unlocked the door and went quietly downstairs to welcome his guests, whom he knew would be gathering in the drawing room.

A cheer went up from every animal in the room as he walked in, and they swarmed around him with congratulations and kind words about how brave he had been, how clever, and what a fighter. Toad merely gave a faint smile and murmured, “Not at all!” Now and then, just for variety, he said, “On the contrary!” Otter was standing on the hearthrug, explaining to a circle of admiring friends precisely how he would have handled everything if only he had been there. Seeing Toad, he burst forward with a shout, flung an arm around his neck, and tried to march him around the room like a conquering hero. Toad, in his mild way, turned rather frosty toward him, and said gently as he slipped free, “Badger was the mastermind; Mole and Water Rat took the worst of the fighting; I simply served in the ranks and did little or nothing.” The animals were clearly baffled and thrown off balance by this surprising new manner. As for Toad, he could feel, while he drifted from guest to guest handing out his modest replies, that everyone found him utterly fascinating.

Badger had ordered the very best of everything, and the banquet was a great success. There was a lot of talk and laughter and teasing among the animals, but through it all Toad, who of course sat in the chair at the head of the table, kept his nose in the air and murmured pleasant nothings to the animals on either side of him. Every so often he stole a glance at Badger and Rat, and each time he looked, they were staring at each other with their mouths hanging open, which gave him the greatest satisfaction. As the evening wore on, some of the younger and livelier animals began whispering to each other that things weren’t as amusing as they used to be in the good old days; and there were some knockings on the table and cries of “Toad! Speech! Speech from Toad! Song! Mr. Toad’s song!” But Toad only shook his head gently and raised one paw in mild protest, and by pressing delicacies on his guests, making topical small talk, and earnestly asking after family members not yet old enough to attend social events, he managed to convey that this dinner was being run on strictly conventional lines.
He was truly a changed Toad!

With that climax behind them, the four friends settled back into the lives that civil war had so rudely interrupted, and they were happy and content, with no more uprisings or invasions to trouble them. Toad talked it over with his friends and picked out a handsome gold chain and a locket set with pearls. He sent it to the jailer’s daughter along with a letter that even Badger had to admit was modest, grateful, and appreciative. The engine-driver, too, got his proper thanks and was paid back for all his trouble. Badger put heavy pressure on Toad, and as a result even the barge-woman was hunted down, after some effort, and quietly repaid what her horse was worth. Toad kicked up a dreadful fuss about this, since he considered himself an instrument of Fate, sent to punish fat women with mottled arms who could not spot a true gentleman when one stood before them. In fact the sum was not very heavy, because the local assessors agreed that the gypsy’s price for the horse was about right.

On long summer evenings the friends would sometimes stroll together through the Wild Wood, which had now been tamed, as far as they were concerned. It was a pleasure to see how respectfully the woodland folk greeted them. The weasel mothers would lead their little ones to the doorways of their holes and point, saying, “Look, baby! There goes the great Mr. Toad! And that’s the gallant Water Rat walking beside him, a terrible fighter! And over there comes the famous Mr. Mole, the one your father is always telling you about!” When the babies were cranky and completely out of hand, though, the mothers would calm them down by warning that if they did not hush up and stop their fussing, the terrible gray Badger would come and carry them off. This was a shameful slander against Badger, who may not have cared much for Society but was rather fond of children. It never failed to do the trick all the same.
